scope: Single engine-assisted exact-move fork review before candidate results

cases.rationale: bxc3 removes the knight and preserves the attacking side's original targets.
f3 or Kg1 keeps the rook, with the queen leaving the attack.
Qf2+ gives check and attacks the f3 bishop, but both separate lines introduce Rd3 and a secondary mechanism.
Qd7+ checks the king to take the g7 bishop. Kc5 allows Qxg7; Kc4 loses g7 to Bxg7 after a forcing exchange.
Nf4 attacks queen e2 and knight d3, which the replies separate. Nxf4 permits Bxe2; Qc2 loses d3 in the exchange sequence.
Qxe3 fxe3 is an even queen exchange and the attacked knight survives.
Bxd4 neutralizes the pawn without cost. Bf2 would allow dxc3 by choice.
The two attacking branches develop kingside and back-rank tactics. The separate role of the two attacked pieces is unclear.
Nxb6 removes the knight and keeps the original targets.
Nf5 forces a knight exchange and the eventual winning plan goes via the c-file and queen. An exact fork payoff is unclear.
Bxe4 removes the queen and keeps the other bishop.
Both principal defences admit an equal queen exchange rather than loss of a target.
Qxe1 safely removes the rook, and the attacked queen is kept.
Bxg7 takes the queen and prevents its fork from gaining material.
After Kh2 the relevant continuation starts with Qxd4 by the queen. The checking rook's d1 attack does not secure a gain.
Qxe2 is answered by an equal recapture in both leading branches. The bishop attack does not win material.
The bishop is captured by queen or bishop and Qxd8+ saves by perpetual. The original fork geometry is incidental.
Nd7+ attacks king and queen. Both king moves allow Nxb8 and Rxb8, winning the queen for a knight.
Either pawn recapture removes the forking knight and keeps both original attacked pieces.
Rb8 and Rc7 hold the apparent threats. The queen moves without a collection.
Either knight takes d4; repeated exchanges settle without material gain.
Na3 attacks the b1 rook and c2 queen. Rxa3 Bxa3 loses the exchange; Qb2 Nxb1 also loses the exchange.
Nxc5 simply removes the knight. The lower ranked lines may lose material by choice.
Qc7 attacks the a5 knight and d8 rook, but Nc6 and its interleaved checks leave a profitable second arm unestablished.
Qxc2 or Nxc2 removes the rook. Bxd4 or Bxb2 belongs to a different piece and mechanism.
Nxd5 removes the attacker in the strongest reply. Nxf4 trades a piece for a piece when allowed.
Ne6+ checks the king and attacks the f8 rook. Both king moves allow Nxf8 Kxf8, winning a rook for the knight.
Ng5 creates a king attack and the nominal fork loses its material value.
Nf6 threatens the e8 rook and e4 bishop. The Bxc6 line includes the delayed Nxe8; the f-pawn move allows Nxe8 immediately.
Ngf4 leads to captures by several pieces while Ngf8 avoids the knight payoff. The initial fork's role is unclear.
